title: A finite-type group scheme over a field has an ample invertible module
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $G$ be a group scheme over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme] whose structure morphism is separated and of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion. There exists an invertible $\mathcal O_G$-module $M$ [def-sc-invertible-module] that is ample in the absolute sense [def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module]. No properness, smoothness, connectedness or commutativity hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 0BF7, lemma-algebraic-quasi-projective: every algebraic group scheme over a field is quasi-projective; over Spec(k), Morphisms Definition 01VW (definition-quasi-projective) and Lemma 01VK (lemma-ample-over-affine) identify this with the existence of an absolutely ample invertible module. The proof of 0BF7 constructs such a module and handles nonreduced and disconnected groups.

proof.text: First work over an algebraically closed field $k$. Put $C=G^0$ and $H=C_{\mathrm{red}}$. The identity-component lemma gives that $C$ is a finite-type open and closed subgroup and that $H$ is smooth, integral, separated and of finite type. Apply the parameter-family lemma to $H$, obtaining $V,\mathcal M,(s_v)$. Applying its last assertion to the identity point of $H$ gives a point $v_0\in V(k)$. Set $L=\mathcal M_{v_0}$. It is invertible because tensor pullback preserves invertibility.

Smoothness of $H$ makes it normal, so the affine-parameter Picard lemma gives isomorphisms $\phi_v:\mathcal M_v\simeq L$ for all $v\in V(k)$. Transfer $s_v$ to $t_v=\phi_v(s_v)$. On each residue-field fibre $\phi_v$ is a linear isomorphism, hence $H_{t_v}=H_{s_v}$, which is affine. Every closed point of $H$ is $k$-rational and thus lies in one of these opens. Their union is all of $H$: otherwise its nonempty closed complement has a closed point by the Jacobson lemma, a contradiction. Since $H$ is finite type over $k$, it is quasi-compact, and these sections with exponent $1$ verify exactly the absolute ampleness definition for $L$.

If $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, the finite-type scheme $C$ is Noetherian (the field is Noetherian since its only ideals are $(0)$ and $(1)$). The characteristic-$p$ reduction lemma therefore lifts existence of an ample invertible module from $H=C_{\mathrm{red}}$ to $C$. If $\operatorname{char}k=0$, Cartier gives that $C$ itself is reduced, so $C=H$ and $L$ is already a module on $C$. In both cases choose an ample invertible module $N$ on $C$.

The component-translation lemma expresses $G$ as finitely many pairwise disjoint open and closed schemes $D_i$, each isomorphic to $C$. Transfer $N$ along these isomorphisms and glue the resulting modules on the disjoint cover, obtaining an invertible module $M$ on $G$. For $x\in D_i$, choose $n\geq1$ and an affine nonvanishing section locus for $N^{\otimes n}$ at the corresponding point of $C$. Transfer its section to $D_i$ and extend it by the zero section on all other $D_j$. The resulting global section of $M^{\otimes n}$ has exactly that affine nonvanishing locus, contained in $D_i$. As $G$ is quasi-compact by finite type, this proves $M$ ample directly from the definition.

For the original field $k$, choose an algebraic closure $\bar k$. Base-change the multiplication, identity and inverse to give $G_{\bar k}$ its group structure; their identities are preserved by the fibre-product universal property. The separated finite-type base-change lemma ensures that $G_{\bar k}$ has the hypotheses of the algebraically closed case proved in Steps 1--4. It therefore admits an absolutely ample invertible module. The field-extension existence-descent lemma, with $X=G$ and $K=\bar k$, now supplies such a module on $G$. This descends existence, and does not assume descent data on the chosen module upstairs.

No repair note exists, so this is a first split of NV's unsplit supporting node, and the statement is unchanged and matches 0BF7 (absolute 01PS ampleness). Step 1: the identity-component node gives exactly the hypotheses of the family node; v0 comes from its covering clause at e, and invertibility from pullback-tensor clause (1). Step 2: smooth implies normal; the 0BEH node then applies (H integral, separated, finite type, normal; V open in A^d). Nonvanishing loci are preserved, and closed points are rational and Jacobson-dense, which gives the 01PS check with n=1. Step 3: char p uses C Noetherian by finite type over a field plus the 0BD4(3) node (pO_C=0 is implicit but one line); char 0 uses the Cartier node to get C reduced, so C=H. Step 4: finitely many translate components that are open and closed, glued, with sections extended by zero; this is elementary. Step 5: algebraic closure, then the base-change leaf, then 0BDC existence descent. proof_deps equals the union of uses, and there is no cycle. The new nodes are all true and match their sources. I tested the family node with H=Spec k (d=0, D empty), 0BEH with n=0 and p=q, Cartier against alpha_p (excluded), the reduction node with k[e]/e^2, and 0BDC with K=k and X empty. None is a duplicate: the geometrically-reduced-smooth, identity-component, ample-on-reduction, finite-normal-ample-descent, very-ample-descends and abelian-variety-projective nodes are all different, and no new node restates an item clause.
